new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Kadugli-Krongo (Kadu) group as a whole, Stevenson says stress ('dynamic accent') is more prominent than pitch, that both tone and stress can be lexically distinctive (Krongo minimal pair differing in stress position), that stress can geminate a following consonant and delete unstressed vowels; the one Tulishi-cluster datum is Kamdang ta-m'dədək 'smith' with stress on the stem-initial syllable after the number prefix. He states no rule for the position of stress, and nothing specific to Tulishi proper.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the Krongo doublet 'kûrùgù / ku'rûgù implies stress position is not fully predictable at least in Krongo.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level generalisation (Kadugli-Krongo), illustrated mainly from Katcha with one Kamdang (= Kamda dialect of Tulishi [tey], Glottolog kamd1238) example; citation forms from Stevenson's 1940s-50s survey fieldwork. Accessed only as Google Books snippets (scanned-degraded diacritics), not as a page image.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress-related datum tied to this glottocode concerns KAMDANG (= Kamda, Glottolog dialect kamd1238 under Tulishi tuli1249; ISO treats Kamda as a Tulishi [tey] dialect), and the statement itself is a group-level generalisation over Kadugli-Krongo illustrated mainly from Katcha (xtc). Hall & Hall 2004 and Hall 2006 likewise describe Kamda, not Tulishi proper (Nuclear Tulishi nucl1437) or Dar el Kabira.

new_statements.relation_note: Same content as the existing Stevenson 1957 statement (it is an explicit paraphrase of Stevenson: 'tone is less important than stress', tonal doublets, Krongo stress-tone doublet), second-hand and at group level; adds no placement rule and nothing Tulishi-specific. The archive.org item is access-restricted (lending library): and are private (download -> not reachable by automated download), fulltext/inside.php -> 403 'Item not available'; the scanned diacritics in the search snippets are garbled ('of5', ''Sf3, 'ku'rigt'), so this text should be checked against a print copy (Harvard Widener 2235.4.26) before any of it is quoted on the site.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level (Kadugli-Krongo as a whole, examples from Katcha and Krongo): stress is said to matter more than tone, stress location can be lexically distinctive (Krongo 'korugut vs ku'rigt) and interacts with tone and consonant length; no statement of where word stress falls and nothing on Tulishi stress specifically.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only Tulishi-specific remark is morphological (many nouns have a non-prefix initial k)
new_statements.identity_note: Schadeberg 1994 lists the language as '1. Mudo: Stevenson "Tulishi", dialect of Kamdang' (informant born 1950 at J. Kamdang), i.e. the Kamda/Kamdang dialect of Tulishi, not Tulishi proper; his tone statement is made for the Kadu group as a whole. Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 19 is group-level (examples from Katcha unless stated; the stress-tone doublet is Krongo), listing TULISHI only as a Western member and for the initial-k noun remark.

readall_conflicts: The two opened works pull in different directions without contradicting each other outright. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (following Stevenson 1956-57) present the Kadugli-Krongo group as having both stress and tone, with dynamic stress 'more important' than tone and stress location lexically distinctive in Krongo; Schadeberg 1994, working from his own 1974-75 field data including the Tulishi/Kamdang ('Mudo') list, treats all Kadu languages as 'almost certainly tone languages' with a two-tone system plus downstep and never mentions stress at all, and the later sources already held by the project (Hall & Hall 2004: two tones, some mid pitch in Kamda; Mullan 2022 citing Hall 2006: three tones in Kamda; Dafalla 2006 snippets: 'certainly tonal.. two tones plus downstep') follow Schadeberg's tonal analysis. None of the sources, old or new, states where word stress falls in Tulishi; the only stress example from the Tulishi area is Stevenson's Kamdang vowel-loss example (ta-m'dədək 'smith') already recorded.
